chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding a man who prays while wearing an iron ring, he said: 'No, and the man should not wear it as a ring, for it is from the clothing of the people of the Fire.'
And he said: 'The man should not wear gold, nor pray in it, because it is from the clothing of the people of Paradise.'
And regarding a garment whose border is silk, he said: 'He should not pray in it.'
And regarding a garment that has an image of a bird or something else in its border, [it was asked]: Should he pray in it? He said: 'No.'

And regarding a soiled spot that is in the house or elsewhere, where the sun has not hit it, but the soiled spot has dried, he said: 'He should not pray on it, and he should know its location until he washes it.'
And regarding the sun, does it purify the ground? He said: 'If the spot is soiled from urine or something else, and the sun hits it and then the spot dries, then praying on the spot is permissible.'
And if the sun hits it but the soiled spot has not dried and is moist, then praying on it is not permissible until it dries.
And if your foot is moist or your forehead is moist or something else from you hits that soiled spot, then do not pray on that spot until it dries, for that is not permissible.
And regarding a man who performs ablution and walks barefoot with his foot moist, he said: 'If your ground is paved, walking on it is sufficient for you.'
And he said: 'As for us, it is permissible for us because our ground is paved, meaning covered with pebbles.'
And regarding a man who wears a ring that has an engraving of an image of a bird or something else, he said: 'Praying in it is not permissible.'

key_terms.لِبَاسُ أَهْلِ النَّارِ: Clothing of the people of the Fire

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for prayer validity regarding clothing materials, gold, silk, and soiled ground?
ai.summary: Compiled by Shaykh al-Tusi in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith systematically categorizes the validity of prayer (*salat*) by addressing both external adornments and environmental purity. It establishes a theological dichotomy where gold and silk are reserved for Paradise, while iron signifies the Fire, and extends these principles to practical jurisprudence regarding soiled ground (*al-mawdi' al-qadhir*) and the sufficiency of sun-drying for purification. The text also clarifies the distinction between paved surfaces and natural gravel, reflecting the specific living conditions of the Imams in Medina.
